topic: Discovery stories / peptides your body makes: glucagon, the pancreas's own blood-sugar raiser, first found as an impurity. Discovered as an impurity in early insulin preparations, a 'toxic fraction' causing a rise in blood glucose; Kimball and Murlin named it glucagon (GLUCose-AGONist); 29-amino-acid peptide made by pancreatic alpha cells; hypoglycaemia triggers release; raises blood glucose via glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis (Scott & Bloom, Peptides 2018); Kimball & Murlin 1923; alpha cells identified as source in 1948; acts in opposition to insulin (A century of glucagon, Nat Rev Endocrinol 2023); primary structure determined 1957 by Bromer et al. at Lilly (Conlon, Front Endocrinol 2021)

Found by accident · 1923

Your pancreas makes a hormone that raises blood sugar.

Early 1920s

A “toxic” impurity

Early insulin extracts from the pancreas had an impurity.

It pushed blood sugar up, not down.

1923: a name

Glucagon

GLUCose AGONist

1948Origin found: alpha cells in the pancreas
1957Structure: 29 amino acids

Its everyday job

Blood sugar falls.

Glucagon tells the liver to:

1Break down stored glycogen
2Make new glucose

Both from your pancreas
Insulin ↓
Lowers blood sugar
Glucagon ↑
Raises blood sugar
